# What Is Selling Time, and Why Do Sellers Spend So Little of It Selling?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seller-time-to-sell/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Selling time is the share of a seller's working week spent directly engaging prospects and clients: prospecting, meetings, calls and correspondence with buyers. Large surveys put it at roughly 30% to 40% of the week. The rest goes to administration, internal coordination, data entry and searching for information, most of which can be reduced by better process before any AI tool is added.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Salesforce's sixth State of Sales report, a survey of 5,500 sales professionals in 27 countries, found 70% of sellers' time went to non-selling tasks.
- In that survey, customer-facing time broke down as about 8% prospecting, 9% virtual customer contact and 12% in-person meetings.
- Salesforce's 2026 survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals put the global average at 40% of time spent selling, and 35% for Gen Z sellers.
- Gen Z sellers in the 2026 survey lost about two hours a week to manual data entry.
- Gartner reported in 2020 that buyers spend only 17% of their purchase time meeting potential suppliers, so the seller time that does exist must count.

## What selling time means

Selling time is a simple ratio: hours spent engaging buyers divided by total working hours. "Engaging buyers" usually includes prospecting, discovery calls, meetings, demonstrations, proposals discussed with the client and follow-up correspondence. It excludes internal meetings, CRM updates, approvals, research done alone and travel, though some surveys count travel within in-person meetings.

The measure matters because it is the capacity of the sales team. A firm with ten sellers at 30% selling time has the equivalent of three full-time sellers in front of clients.

| Counts as selling time | Does not count |
| --- | --- |
| Prospecting calls and emails | Updating CRM fields |
| Discovery and needs meetings | Internal pipeline reviews |
| Proposal walk-throughs with the buyer | Writing proposals alone |
| Negotiation and closing calls | Deal desk and approval chasing |
| Client check-ins and renewals | Searching for content or past work |

## Why sellers spend so little of it selling

### The numbers have been stable for years

Salesforce's sixth State of Sales report surveyed 5,500 sales professionals across 27 countries. As reported by diginomica in August 2024, it found 70% of working time went to non-sales tasks. Customer-facing time split into roughly 8% prospecting, 9% virtual customer contact and 12% in-person meetings including travel.

Salesforce's 2026 report, a survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals, put the global average at 40% of time spent selling. Gen Z sellers spent 35%, and lost about two hours a week to manual data entry. The two surveys use different samples, so the change between them should not be read as a precise trend. Both are vendor-run, by a company that sells CRM and AI tools.

### Where the rest goes

The causes are mostly structural, not individual:

1. **Data entry.** Logging calls, emails and meetings by hand, often twice.
2. **Information search.** Finding the latest proposal, pricing, case study or the history of an account.
3. **Internal coordination.** Approvals, handoffs, pipeline meetings and forecast calls.
4. **Tool switching.** Moving between CRM, email, document storage and messaging.
5. **Unqualified pipeline.** Time spent on deals that should have been disqualified earlier.

### Buyers give sellers little time anyway

Gartner reported in 2020 that buyers considering a purchase spend only 17% of that time meeting potential suppliers, shared across every supplier they consider. Seller time is scarce on both sides. Recovering hours only helps if they go to the right accounts, which is why the ICP and stage definitions matter as much as admin reduction.

## How to recover selling time

The first gains come from process, not tools. AI then helps with the remainder, provided it works from clean records.

| Lever | What it removes | Example action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic capture | Manual activity logging | Turn on email and calendar sync in the CRM |
| Fewer required fields | Form-filling at every stage | Require fields only at stage entry and close |
| Content in one place | Searching for past work | One indexed library of proposals and cases |
| Earlier disqualification | Time on deals that will not close | Written exit criteria for the qualification stage |
| Shorter internal reviews | Status meetings | Review exceptions only, from CRM data |
| Drafting assistance | Writing first drafts of emails and summaries | An assistant at autonomy level 1, drafts only |

Salesforce's 2026 research found 54% of sellers had used AI agents, with nearly nine in ten planning to by 2027. The useful early applications are the boring ones: summarising calls into the CRM, drafting follow-ups and assembling account briefings. In **lowob**'s model, these sit at autonomy level 1, drafting only, and nothing sends without a person. That keeps the time saving without handing judgment to a tool reading imperfect data.

Measure before and after. A two-week time diary for three or four sellers, split into the categories above, gives a baseline that any change can be judged against.

## lowob takeaways

- **Selling time is capacity.** At 30% to 40%, most of a sales team's paid hours are not spent with buyers.
- **The causes are structural.** Data entry, search, coordination and weak qualification account for most lost time.
- **Fix process first.** Automatic capture and fewer required fields recover hours before AI is involved.
- **Use AI to draft, not decide.** The safest early gains come from summaries and drafts a person approves.

## Common questions

### How much time do salespeople actually spend selling?

Salesforce's surveys put it between about 30% and 40% of the working week, with the 2026 global average at 40%.

### What do sales reps spend most of their time on?

Administration, data entry, internal meetings, searching for information and coordinating approvals, according to repeated State of Sales surveys.

### How do you increase selling time?

Automate activity capture, require fewer fields, centralise content, disqualify weak deals earlier and use AI assistants for drafts and summaries.

### Can AI agents give sellers more time to sell?

They can remove drafting and logging work. The gain depends on clean CRM data and a person approving anything sent to a client.
